KCK looking to increase stock of single-family housing

Zoning review coming in response to the “By-Right Housing Development Act,” a state law that took effect July 1.
by Kansas City Documenters
documenters@thebeacon.media
August 21, 2026August 22, 2026

Unified Government of Wyandotte County & Kansas City, Kansas: City Planning Commission (Aug. 10, 2026)

By Masha Mackey, Kansas City Documenter

These notes were produced through Kansas City Documenters, which trains and pays community members to take fact-checked notes at public meetings, strengthening transparency and accountability in local government.

Summary

  • The planning commission unanimously approved the consent agenda and several zoning and special-use permit requests but recommended denial of one short-term rental application. The full agenda is here.
  • Commissioners received a legislative update on Kansas Senate Bill 418, also known as the “By-Right Housing Development Act,” which took effect July 1. Staff outlined changes the UG will need to make to comply with the law.
  • Staff presented an overview of the Downtown Self-Supported Municipal Improvement District (SMID), explaining its governance, funding and role in supporting downtown services and revitalization efforts.
  • For all zoning changes, special-use permits, vacations and preliminary plan reviews on this meeting’s agenda, the planning commission will make recommendations to the Board of Commissioners, which is expected to make final decisions on Aug. 27. For final plots and final plan reviews, the planning commission’s decisions are final.

Notes

Zoning Change

  • 8811 Leavenworth Road
    • The applicant requested rezoning about 5.7 acres from R-1 single family to agricultural to allow small-scale personal farming and livestock, including chickens and goats.
    • Commissioners discussed allowable livestock, accessory structures and conservation district guidance. Planning staff recommended approval, noting agricultural zoning would better accommodate future barns and related structures.

Short-Term Rental Applications

  • 2651 Minnesota Ave.: Approved for one year.
  • 3131 S. 47th St.: Owner-occupied short-term rental approved.
  • 3237 Kimball Ave.: Non-owner-occupied short-term rental approved for one year.
  • 1710 N. 90th St.: Returned to the planning commission after being remanded by the board of commissioners.
    • During discussion of the remanded application, commissioners noted the applicant did not attend despite having been notified. Members also referenced prior neighborhood concerns regarding property management and compatibility with the surrounding neighborhood.
    • The commission voted 4-2 to recommend denial of the application.

Special Use Permit

  • Auto Glass Repair Business – 2810 S. 44th St.
    • Staff clarified the business would perform only glass repair and replacement, with all vehicles stored indoors and no body repairs performed.

Reports

Your source for fact-checked notes from local public meetings. Sign up for the free Kansas City Documenters newsletter.

  • SB 418 Legislative Update
    • A  presentation to the board said that the law is meant to “address statewide housing shortages and promote affordability by streamlining permitting for housing development.”
    • Mike Farley, an attorney with the UG, explained the law’s provisions and discussed changes the UG will have to make to comply with the law. Provisions Farley highlighted included:
      • A house can be built on a lot as small as 3,000 square feet and is only required to have a single-car garage. The minimum lot size the UG currently allows is 5,000 square feet. Farley said the UG’s current code is apparently consistent with the garage requirements.
      • Governmental bodies are not required to provide written notice to nearby neighbors when a property owner requests a rezoning to single-family residential. Also, in those instances, petitioners are not allowed to protest planning commission recommendations.
        • The Board of Commissioners will need six votes to approve the planning commission recommendation and eight votes to override it.
      • The government has 60 days to review plat requests and gets an additional 30 days in instances where the request is for 40 or more units. The UG is going to have to make provisions for this expedited review process.
      • Single-family housing is allowed in any zoning district that already allows for residential. The UG does have one zoning district that allows for some residential but not single-family.
        • Current zoning regulations for accessory dwelling units (ADU) comply with SB 418. 
        • According to the staff presentation, ADUs “provide opportunities for rental spaces or multigenerational living arrangements that expand housing options for Wyandotte County residents that support closing the housing gap across several demographics.”
        • SB 418 complements UG efforts already underway to expand eligibility for ADUs.
      • Staff hopes to present an ordinance to the commission next month that would make zoning changes necessary for the UG to comply with SB 418.
KCK zoning is shifting fast. Keep Documenters in the room. Give now

Downtown SMID Presentation

  • The SMID is funded through a property tax levied within the district. Its current authorization runs through the end of this year.
  • The presenter was Dawn Rattan, executive director of the Downtown Shareholders of Kansas City Kansas. She said:
    • The district was established in 2008. It has an advisory board appointed by the board of commissioners. Its north-south boundaries run from Washington Boulevard to Tauromee Avenue, and its east-west boundaries run from Third Street to 12th Street.
    • Services include cleaning, security, marketing, placemaking and downtown beautification. The board has increased funding for biohazard cleaning at the request of businesses, Rattan said, “because our current contractor can’t clean bodily waste.”
    • The SMID pays for a dedicated police officer.
    • “We just want to bring downtown KCK back,” Rattan said. “Nationally, all around the country, places like Detroit have seen major comebacks in downtown. A lot of times, in downtown, this is where you have your small-business owners. You don’t have a lot of chains, so this is a tribute to entrepreneurship, and it really is the soul of the city.”
    • Recent activities include holding a mayoral forum. SMID has a grant to take better pictures of downtown, and it is initiating some facade improvements.
    • Priorities include repainting crosswalks at Seventh Street and Minnesota Avenue and turning a vacant space into a business incubator. They also want an updated master plan that could help determine how to compete with online shopping, and board members would like to see about refreshing the upstairs of buildings into living spaces for younger residents.
    • “And of course, the Reardon Center keeps popping up,” Rattan said. “Everyone wants to know what’s going to be done with the Reardon Center.” The boarded up Jack Reardon Conference Center has been the subject of on-again-off-again redevelopment plans for several years. The center is located at Fifth Street and Minnesota Avenue.
  • The planning commission found that renewal of the SMID is consistent with the city’s comprehensive plan, and forwarded its recommendation to the UG board of commissioners. 

Observations

  • Most agenda items were approved unanimously with little discussion, while the remanded short-term rental generated the most deliberation because of prior neighborhood concerns and the applicant’s absence.
  • Beyond individual zoning cases, much of the meeting focused on preparing for implementation of SB 418 and its anticipated effect on future zoning and development processes.
  • The SMID presentation emphasized continued investment in downtown revitalization through public-private partnerships, maintenance and marketing initiatives.

Follow-Up Questions

  • When will the commission consider the zoning code amendments required by SB 418?
  • How will the UG balance the new by-right housing requirements with existing neighborhood planning goals?
  • Will additional guidance or performance measures be developed for future short-term rental applications following the commissioners’ discussion of neighborhood compatibility?
  • How will residents react when they find out they cannot appeal decisions made by the planning commission?
